summary: Latvia is part of the Schengen Area: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely, around 60 visa-exempt nationalities get 90 days in any 180-day period (with ETIAS being phased in), and everyone else needs a €90 Schengen short-stay visa. Russian citizens with Schengen tourist visas are refused entry, and land borders with Russia and Belarus are heavily restricted.

defaultStayWindow.text: 90 days in any rolling 180-day period, counted across the whole Schengen Area rather than per country. The day you arrive counts as the first day and the day you leave counts as the last. Leaving and coming back does not reset the allowance: on any given day, days already spent anywhere in the area during the preceding 180 still count against the 90.

fee.notes: Children 6–11: €45; under 6: free. Fee set EU-wide since June 11, 2024.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Latvia — visa information

fee.notes: Approximate — for employment, study and other stays over 90 days, usually alongside a residence-permit process. Confirm the current fee and requirements with the Latvian mission.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Latvia — visa information

passportValidity.text: Non-EU passports must be valid for at least 3 months beyond your planned departure from the Schengen Area and have been issued within the last 10 years.

travelInsurance.text: Schengen visa applicants must hold travel medical insurance covering at least €30,000, valid across the Schengen Area for the whole stay. Visa-exempt visitors are not required to show it but border officers may ask about cover.

onwardTicket.text: Border officers may ask non-EU visitors for proof of return or onward travel and accommodation details.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Latvia — visa information

proofOfFunds.text: Latvia’s published guideline is modest — around €14 per person per day — but officers assess sufficiency case by case together with accommodation and tickets. Confirm the current figure with the Latvian mission.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Latvia — visa information

declarations.name: EES — Entry/Exit System (biometric registration)
declarations.submitWindow: At the border on first entry
declarations.text: Non-EU travelers are registered biometrically (fingerprints and photo) in the EU Entry/Exit System at Schengen external borders. Registration happens at the border. There is nothing to submit in advance, but allow extra time on your first entry.

declarations.name: ETIAS — European Travel Information and Authorization System

fee.notes: Free for under-18s and over-70s. Valid 3 years or until passport expiry.

declarations.text: Visa-exempt travelers will need an ETIAS travel authorization to enter the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU site for the current status and apply only there.

currencyLimits.text: Cash of €10,000 or more (or equivalent) must be declared when entering or leaving the EU.

notes: Duty-free from outside the EU: 200 cigarettes, 1 liter of spirits, goods up to €300 (€430 arriving by air/sea).
No limits on goods for personal use when arriving from another EU country.

payments.text: Cards and contactless payments are accepted almost everywhere in Latvia, including Riga’s Central Market stalls; a little cash is only occasionally useful in the countryside.

safety.text: Latvia is a safe destination with low violent crime. Watch for pickpocketing and overpriced-bar scams in Riga’s Old Town nightlife, and take care on icy pavements in winter.

source.name: U.S. Department of State — Latvia Travel Advisory

bestTimeToVisit.text: May–September is best for Riga, the Jūrmala beaches and Gauja National Park; December brings atmospheric Christmas markets — Riga claims the world’s first decorated Christmas tree.

idp.text: Latvia is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

driving.text: Latvia is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Latvia yet.

tips.text: Do not plan overland travel into or out of Russia or Belarus: crossings are heavily restricted or closed, and Russian citizens with Schengen visas issued for tourism are refused entry to Latvia.

Non-EU visitors are registered biometrically in the EU Entry/Exit System at the border, and the ETIAS travel authorization is being phased in for visa-exempt travelers. Check the official EU site before you fly.
In Riga’s Old Town nightlife, stick to venues you chose yourself. The classic scam is a friendly invitation to a bar followed by an extortionate bill.
Latvia sits at the center of the Baltic loop — comfortable buses link Riga with Tallinn and Vilnius in about 4 hours each; all three are Schengen, so the 90/180-day allowance is shared, not reset.
From November to March pack warm layers and shoes with grip — pavements ice over, daylight is short, and many sights keep reduced winter hours.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Latvia?
faq.answer: EU and EFTA citizens enter freely with a passport or ID card. Citizens of around 60 countries — including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan — can visit visa-free for 90 days in any 180-day period. Everyone else needs a Schengen short-stay visa (€90) from a Latvian mission or visa center.

faq.question: Does time in Latvia count against my Schengen 90-day limit?
faq.answer: Yes. Latvia is fully in the Schengen Area, so days spent there count toward the single 90-days-in-180 allowance shared with all other Schengen countries, including Estonia and Lithuania.

faq.question: Can Russian citizens enter Latvia with a Schengen visa?
faq.answer: Generally no. Latvia refuses entry to Russian citizens holding Schengen visas issued for tourism, and land borders with Russia and Belarus are heavily restricted. Narrow exemptions exist for residents, family members of EU citizens and humanitarian cases. Check with the Latvian authorities before traveling.

faq.question: Do I need ETIAS to visit Latvia?
faq.answer: Once ETIAS becomes mandatory, visa-exempt non-EU travelers will need the €20 online authorization before traveling to Latvia and the rest of the Schengen Area. It is being phased in. Check the official EU ETIAS site for the current status.

faq.question: Can I visit all three Baltic states on one Schengen visa?
faq.answer: Yes — Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are all in the Schengen Area, so a single Schengen visa (or your visa-free allowance) covers the whole Baltic circuit with no internal border checks.
